notes: Where the lidar and the two cameras sit relative to each other. HAND-MEASURED,
not fitted -- these are the numbers to edit when something is re-bolted, and
test/test_lidar_overlay.py is how you check them against a real image.
FRAME. Everything is expressed in the RIG frame, which uses the same axis
convention as the camera frame already on the wire (see protocol.py ray_cam):
+x starboard (right)   +y DOWN   +z forward
Note +y is DOWN, so a camera mounted above the lidar has a NEGATIVE y.
By default the rig frame is the lidar's own frame (the lidar pose below is all
zeros), because the mounting was measured from the lidar's centre. Give the
lidar a pose if you later define a boat datum somewhere else -- everything
downstream goes through the same transform either way.
POSE. Each entry is the pose of that body IN the rig frame:
p_rig = R(yaw,pitch,roll) @ p_body + xyz_m
Angles in degrees, applied yaw*pitch*roll (roll first):
yaw   about +y (down)     positive swings to STARBOARD
pitch about +x (right)    positive is NOSE UP
roll  about +z (forward)  positive puts STARBOARD DOWN
CAMERAS. BACK TO BACK, not both looking forward. Each faces its own beam and
is turned 15 deg toward the bow, so their axes are 180-15-15 = 150 deg apart
and their fields meet across the bow instead of overlapping almost entirely.
cam0 looks to PORT (yaw -75), cam1 to STARBOARD (yaw +75). Each sits about
5 cm from the lidar centre along its own pointing direction and about 5 cm
above the scan plane -- the height is what stops the camera body blocking the
lidar. cam0 and cam1 are written out in full rather than mirrored so each can
absorb its own mounting error independently.
This file said 15 deg either side of FORWARD until 2026-08-08, which put both
cameras 90 deg from where they actually are and had them the wrong way round.
Nothing failed: the fit was fine, every projection landed inside a frame, and
the sweep came out fully coloured -- from the wrong lens. cam1 is the physical
STARBOARD camera, confirmed by shining a green light into it and finding the
colour on the PORT half of the plot, which is exactly what a pose 150 deg out
does. The 150 deg figure is the mounting as described by hand; the two yaws
below are that figure split evenly about the beam, so VERIFY THEM with
test/test_lidar_overlay.py --cam 0 --yaw N before trusting a bearing. The
cameras do not overlap enough to register against each other (measured: no
correlation peak), so the lidar is the only thing that can tie them together.
The cameras are inverted and the pipeline rotates 180 deg before anything else
sees the frame, so the calibration, the images and these poses are all in the
same upright frame. There is no extra flip to apply here.
SANITY. The lidar plane sits 5 cm below the lens, so returns land slightly
below the horizon row and converge onto it with range: at 0.5 m a return is
about 50 net px below the axis, at 3 m about 6, at 12 m under 2. If your
overlay shows the opposite trend, y has the wrong sign.

_yaw: STALE since the unit was remounted upside down (2026-08-08) -- see _angle
below for the half of this that changed with confidence. This -45 was
measured for the OLD, right-side-up mount: its own 0 mark pointed 45 deg to
port, and -45 turned that back onto the rig's forward.
A remount changes which physical direction the 0 mark points, and by how
much depends on WHICH horizontal axis it was flipped about -- rolled over
(0 mark mirrors port<->starboard, new yaw is the simple sign flip, +45) is a
different answer from pitched over (0 mark mirrors fore<->aft, new yaw is
nowhere near +45). Guessing between them would be exactly the invented
hardware number this repo's docs say not to publish, so this is left at the
OLD, now-wrong value rather than a fabricated new one -- do not trust the
front lidar's bearing (or its colouring, which projects through this same
geometry) until it is remeasured.
One measurement fixes it: put a target dead ahead, read its RAW reported_deg
in test_lidar_overlay.py (angle_zero_deg is 0, so that reading needs no
correction itself), and with angle_dir now -1 below,
yaw_deg = reported_deg_dead_ahead
makes rig bearing 0 for that target. Check the sign before trusting it, same
as always: dead ahead should read near 0 deg in the overlay tool and near
the top of the receiver's top-down plot.
_angle: How the C1's reported heading becomes a direction in the rig frame:
so a = 0 is forward (+z) and a grows toward starboard (+x).
angle_dir is +1 for the C1's clockwise-from-above convention and -1 if your
unit or mounting runs the other way; angle_zero_deg rotates the sensor's own
Flipped to -1 on 2026-08-08: the unit was remounted upside down, and turning
a rotationally-symmetric sensor over reverses the rotation's apparent
chirality as seen from the rig's fixed 'above' (-y) reference, regardless of
which horizontal axis the flip was about -- unlike the yaw fix above, this
one direction argument holds no matter how it was physically flipped.
VERIFY ANYWAY with the overlay tool rather than trusting it -- nothing here
has been run against hardware since the remount, and a sign error on this
specific flag looks like a plausible but mirrored world, which is the
failure most likely to survive a casual glance.

_self_box: THE BOAT ITSELF. A 360 deg planar scanner on the bow sees the vessel it is
bolted to: the superstructure, the mast, the aft lidar's housing and anything
stowed on deck all come back as solid returns at 1-3 m, and to a range-only
sensor those are indistinguishable from a mark that close. Every return inside
this box is discarded in fusion.fuse before anything projects, colours or
ranges it, and the count ships as `n_self`.
The box is in the RIG frame (+x starboard, +z forward), so a return is the
boat when
|x| <= half_width_m   and   back_m <= z <= front_m
half_width_m is EITHER SIDE of the centreline, so 0.70 is a 1.40 m corridor.
front_m 0.0 is the lidar's own plane: the box starts at the sensor and runs
AFT. back_m null means no rear edge, because the hull and the deck run astern
and no measured length says where they stop -- an open corridor astern is the
same statement drop_unseen already makes, that the AFT lidar owns behind.
These are the requested dimensions, NOT measured against the hull, and they
are worth checking on the boat before they are trusted: with the mask off
(sender.py --no-lidar-self-box) the deck's returns are visible on the
receiver's top-down plot, and the box should cover them and nothing else.
IT DEPENDS ON THE LIDAR YAW ABOVE, which is STALE. `aft` here means -z in the
rig frame, and which physical direction that is comes entirely from
lidar.yaw_deg -- so while that number is the pre-remount value, this box is
pointing 90-ish deg away from the stern and is masking open water instead of
the deck. Remeasure the yaw first; the box only means what it says once it is
right. Set this to false to switch the mask off for a rig that does not need
it (a sensor that sees no part of its own vessel).
_cams: xyz is 5 cm along each camera's own pointing direction, per the rule above:
0.05 * (sin(yaw), 0, cos(yaw)) with y = -0.05 for the height over the scan
plane. It moved with the yaw because it is derived from it, not measured
separately. At 2-12 m a 5 cm baseline is worth under 1.5 deg anyway -- the
yaw is what decides whether colour lands on the right return, not this.

cam0._note: PORT-facing. Was +15.0 (assumed forward-looking); see the header.
